categories.description: Places, journeys and the geography of the biblical world.

categories.description: Excavations, inscriptions and the material traces of history.

categories.label: People & history
categories.description: Rulers, prophets and the beginnings of the church.

leaders.name: Heinrich Bullinger
leaders.line: Zwingli's successor in Zürich for 44 years; his Decades of sermons were read across Europe.

leaders.name: John Calvin
leaders.line: French reformer who taught and preached in Geneva; author of the Institutes and commentaries on most of the Bible.

leaders.name: John Knox
leaders.line: Scottish reformer; pastor to the English exiles in Geneva, then preacher at St Giles', Edinburgh.

leaders.name: Zacharias Ursinus
leaders.line: Professor at Heidelberg and the main writer of the Heidelberg Catechism (1563).

leaders.name: William Perkins
leaders.line: Cambridge preacher and teacher whose plain-style sermons shaped a generation of Puritans.

leaders.name: William Ames
leaders.line: English Puritan exiled to the Netherlands; professor at Franeker and author of The Marrow of Theology.

leaders.name: Richard Sibbes
leaders.line: Preacher at Gray's Inn, London, and master of St Catharine's, Cambridge; known for The Bruised Reed.

leaders.name: Thomas Goodwin
leaders.line: Puritan preacher, member of the Westminster Assembly and president of Magdalen College, Oxford.

leaders.name: Samuel Rutherford
leaders.line: Scottish minister of Anwoth whose letters, many written in exile in Aberdeen, are still read today.

leaders.name: John Owen
leaders.line: Puritan theologian, dean of Christ Church, Oxford; wrote on sin, the Spirit and Hebrews.

leaders.name: Thomas Watson
leaders.line: Puritan pastor of St Stephen Walbrook, London; author of A Body of Divinity.

leaders.name: Francis Turretin
leaders.line: Professor at Geneva; his Institutes of Elenctic Theology became the textbook at Princeton.

leaders.name: John Flavel
leaders.line: Puritan pastor in the port town of Dartmouth; wrote on providence and the heart.

leaders.name: Stephen Charnock
leaders.line: Puritan preacher in London; best known for The Existence and Attributes of God.

leaders.name: John Bunyan
leaders.line: Tinker and preacher of Bedford, jailed twelve years for preaching; wrote The Pilgrim's Progress.

leaders.name: Herman Witsius
leaders.line: Dutch professor at Franeker, Utrecht and Leiden; wrote The Economy of the Covenants.

leaders.name: Thomas Boston
leaders.line: Scottish minister of Ettrick; wrote Human Nature in its Fourfold State.

leaders.name: John Gill
leaders.line: Baptist pastor in Southwark for 51 years; wrote a verse-by-verse commentary on the whole Bible.

leaders.name: John Wesley
leaders.line: Anglican priest and open-air preacher who led the Methodist revival in Britain for more than fifty years.

leaders.name: Jonathan Edwards
leaders.line: Pastor at Northampton, Massachusetts, during the Great Awakening; philosopher and theologian.

leaders.name: George Whitefield
leaders.line: Open-air preacher of the Great Awakening who crossed the Atlantic thirteen times.

leaders.name: David Brainerd
leaders.line: Missionary to the Delaware people; his diary, edited by Edwards, has never gone out of print.

leaders.name: John Newton
leaders.line: Former slave-ship captain turned pastor of Olney and London; wrote Amazing Grace and many letters.

leaders.name: William Carey
leaders.line: Shoemaker turned missionary; translated the Bible into Bengali and other languages of India.

leaders.name: Archibald Alexander
leaders.line: First professor of Princeton Theological Seminary (1812).

leaders.name: Charles Hodge
leaders.line: Taught some 3,000 students at Princeton Seminary over 56 years; wrote a three-volume Systematic Theology.

leaders.name: Andrew A. Bonar
leaders.line: Scottish minister and friend of McCheyne, whose memoir and sermons he published.

leaders.name: Robert Murray M’Cheyne
leaders.line: Minister of St Peter's, Dundee, who died at 29; his Bible reading plan is still widely used.

leaders.name: J. C. Ryle
leaders.line: Evangelical Anglican writer and the first bishop of Liverpool; wrote Holiness and gospel commentaries.

leaders.name: A. A. Hodge
leaders.line: Charles Hodge's son; missionary in India, pastor in Maryland, Virginia and Pennsylvania, then his father's successor at Princeton.

leaders.name: John G. Paton
leaders.line: Scottish missionary to the New Hebrides (now Vanuatu); his autobiography was a 19th-century best-seller.

leaders.name: Charles Haddon Spurgeon
leaders.line: Baptist pastor of one London congregation for 38 years, in the Metropolitan Tabernacle from 1861; the most widely read preacher of his age.

leaders.name: D. L. Moody
leaders.line: Shoe salesman turned evangelist; led great campaigns in Britain and America from 1873 and in 1886 founded the Chicago Bible institute that now bears his name.

leaders.name: Abraham Kuyper
leaders.line: Dutch theologian, founder of the Free University of Amsterdam and prime minister of the Netherlands.

leaders.name: B. B. Warfield
leaders.line: Princeton professor for 34 years; wrote on the inspiration of Scripture and the person of Christ.

leaders.name: Herman Bavinck
leaders.line: Dutch theologian at Kampen and Amsterdam; wrote the four-volume Reformed Dogmatics.

leaders.name: Geerhardus Vos
leaders.line: Dutch-born professor at Princeton, called the father of Reformed biblical theology.

leaders.name: G. Campbell Morgan
leaders.line: Self-taught English Congregational preacher, twice minister of Westminster Chapel in London, whose expository Bible teaching reached both sides of the Atlantic.

leaders.name: Samuel Marinus Zwemer
leaders.line: Missionary to Arabia and Egypt, called the Apostle to Islam; later professor at Princeton.

leaders.name: Louis Berkhof
leaders.line: Dutch-American professor at Calvin Seminary; his Systematic Theology is still a standard textbook.

leaders.name: J. Gresham Machen
leaders.line: Princeton New Testament scholar who founded Westminster Seminary; wrote Christianity and Liberalism.

leaders.name: John Murray
leaders.line: Scottish theologian who taught at Westminster Seminary for 36 years; wrote Redemption Accomplished and Applied.

leaders.name: D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones
leaders.line: Physician turned preacher; minister of Westminster Chapel, London, for thirty years.

leaders.name: Billy Graham
leaders.line: Southern Baptist evangelist who preached the gospel in person to nearly 215 million people in more than 185 countries and territories.

leaders.name: J. I. Packer
leaders.line: English theologian who taught at Regent College, Vancouver; wrote Knowing God.

leaders.name: R. C. Sproul
leaders.line: Teacher and founder of Ligonier Ministries; wrote The Holiness of God.

leaders.name: John MacArthur
leaders.line: Calvinistic Baptist pastor of the non-denominational Grace Community Church, Sun Valley, California, for 56 years (1969–2025); his verse-by-verse preaching is heard on Grace to You.

leaders.name: D. A. Carson
leaders.line: New Testament scholar at Trinity Evangelical Divinity School and co-founder of The Gospel Coalition.

leaders.name: John Piper
leaders.line: Pastor of Bethlehem Baptist Church, Minneapolis, for 33 years; founder of Desiring God.

leaders.name: Sinclair B. Ferguson
leaders.line: Scottish pastor and theologian; teaching fellow of Ligonier Ministries.

leaders.name: Alistair Begg
leaders.line: Scottish-born pastor of Parkside Church near Cleveland, Ohio; heard daily on Truth For Life.

leaders.name: James R. White
leaders.line: Apologist and director of Alpha and Omega Ministries; known for public debates.

leaders.name: Flavius Josephus
leaders.line: Jewish priest and soldier turned historian; his books are the fullest record of the Jewish world in the time of Jesus and the apostles.
aliases: Flavius Josephus, tr. William Whiston, with Whiston's note 9

leaders.name: Tacitus
leaders.line: Roman senator and historian whose Annals mention Christ's execution under Pontius Pilate.

leaders.name: Pliny the Younger
leaders.line: Roman governor of Bithynia whose letter to the emperor Trajan describes how early Christians worshipped.

leaders.name: Origen of Alexandria
leaders.line: Teacher in Alexandria and Caesarea who set the Hebrew Old Testament beside its Greek versions in six columns.
aliases: Origen (trans. Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 4)
Origen (trans. John Patrick, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 9, ed. Allan Menzies)

leaders.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
leaders.line: Bishop of Caesarea and the first historian of the church; much of what we know of the early church comes through him.
aliases: Eusebius (trans. A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 1)

leaders.name: Jerome
leaders.line: Learned Hebrew to translate the Bible into Latin; his Vulgate was the Bible of the Western church for a thousand years.
aliases: Jerome (trans. E. C. Richardson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 3)
Jerome (trans. W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 2, vol. 6)
Jerome, tr. W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley

leaders.name: Augustine of Hippo
leaders.line: Bishop of Hippo in North Africa; his thought shaped both Catholic and Protestant theology.
aliases: Augustine of Hippo · New Advent edition
Augustine, tr. S. D. F. Salmond
Augustine, tr. S. D. F. Salmond (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 6)

leaders.name: Anselm of Canterbury
leaders.line: Monk and archbishop of Canterbury who asked why God became man.

leaders.name: Thomas Aquinas
leaders.line: Dominican friar and teacher at Paris; the greatest of the medieval scholars, or 'schoolmen'.

leaders.name: Desiderius Erasmus
leaders.line: Dutch scholar who printed the first published Greek New Testament, the text behind Luther's and Tyndale's translations.

leaders.name: William Tyndale
leaders.line: Translated the New Testament into English from the Greek, and was executed for it; much of his wording lives on in the King James Version.

leaders.name: James Ussher
leaders.line: Archbishop of Armagh and scholar who worked out a chronology of the world from Scripture and ancient histories.

leaders.name: William Whiston
leaders.line: Cambridge mathematician whose English translation of Josephus is still the most reprinted one.
aliases: Flavius Josephus, tr. William Whiston, with Whiston's note 9

leaders.name: Edward Robinson
leaders.line: American scholar who travelled Palestine in 1838 and identified many biblical places; called the father of biblical geography.

leaders.name: William Smith
leaders.line: English lexicographer who edited the great Victorian Dictionary of the Bible.

leaders.name: Constantin von Tischendorf
leaders.line: German scholar who found Codex Sinaiticus, the oldest complete New Testament, at St Catherine's Monastery in Sinai.

leaders.name: Roswell D. Hitchcock
leaders.line: Professor at Union Seminary, New York, whose dictionary gives the meaning of nearly every name in the Bible.

leaders.name: Austen Henry Layard
leaders.line: Excavated the Assyrian palaces at Nimrud and Nineveh, publishing reliefs, inscriptions, and accounts of the fieldwork.

leaders.name: Philip Schaff
leaders.line: Swiss-born church historian in America; wrote an eight-volume history of the church and edited the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers in English.

leaders.name: A. R. Fausset
leaders.line: Anglican clergyman, co-author of the Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary and of a Bible encyclopaedia.
aliases: R. Jamieson, A. R. Fausset and D. Brown

leaders.name: James Strong
leaders.line: Methodist professor whose concordance gave every Hebrew and Greek word of the Bible a number, still used everywhere.

leaders.name: M. G. Easton
leaders.line: Scottish minister whose Illustrated Bible Dictionary explains people, places and things of the Bible.

leaders.name: Alfred Edersheim
leaders.line: Vienna-born Jewish convert to Christ who described the Jewish world of the Gospels.

leaders.name: B. F. Westcott
leaders.line: Cambridge professor and bishop of Durham; with Hort he edited a landmark Greek New Testament.

leaders.name: Hormuzd Rassam
leaders.line: Mosul-born archaeologist who excavated at Nineveh, Nimrud, Babylon, and Sippar and recovered major collections of cuneiform tablets.

leaders.name: Joseph Henry Thayer
leaders.line: Harvard professor whose Greek-English lexicon of the New Testament was the standard for decades.

leaders.name: J. B. Lightfoot
leaders.line: Cambridge scholar and bishop of Durham; his commentaries on Paul's letters and his edition of the Apostolic Fathers are classics.

leaders.name: F. J. A. Hort
leaders.line: Cambridge scholar who worked with Westcott for 28 years on the Greek text of the New Testament.

leaders.name: Charles Warren
leaders.line: Surveyed and explored Jerusalem's walls, tunnels, and ancient waterworks for the Palestine Exploration Fund.

leaders.name: George Smith (Assyriologist)
leaders.line: Assyriologist and excavator who identified the Babylonian flood narrative among tablets from Nineveh and published Mesopotamian texts and discoveries.

leaders.name: Orville J. Nave
leaders.line: United States Army chaplain who spent fourteen years gathering the Bible's verses by subject.

leaders.name: James Orr
leaders.line: Scottish theologian who edited the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

leaders.name: S. R. Driver
leaders.line: Oxford Hebrew professor; with Francis Brown and Charles Briggs he made the standard Hebrew lexicon of the Old Testament.

leaders.name: William M. Ramsay
leaders.line: Scottish archaeologist who spent years in Asia Minor and found Luke a careful historian of Paul's journeys.

leaders.name: Flinders Petrie
leaders.line: Excavated Tell el-Hesi and helped establish pottery sequence and stratigraphic dating in Palestinian archaeology.

leaders.name: Robert Koldewey
leaders.line: Directed the German excavations at Babylon, documenting its temples, palaces, fortifications, and the Ishtar Gate.

leaders.name: R. A. Torrey
leaders.line: Evangelist and Bible teacher whose New Topical Text Book gathers the Bible's verses under more than 600 subjects.

leaders.name: Frederick Jones Bliss
leaders.line: Excavated Tell el-Hesi, Jerusalem, and sites in the southern Shephelah for the Palestine Exploration Fund.

leaders.name: A. T. Robertson
leaders.line: Greek scholar at Southern Baptist Seminary; his harmony sets the four Gospels side by side.

leaders.name: James Henry Breasted
leaders.line: Egyptologist whose epigraphic surveys and translations made Egyptian historical inscriptions widely available for studying the ancient Near East.

leaders.name: John Garstang
leaders.line: Led major excavations at Jericho; his chronology and conclusions became a focus of later archaeological reassessment.

leaders.name: Leonard Woolley
leaders.line: Directed the excavations at Ur, documenting the Royal Cemetery, the ziggurat, houses, and the development of ancient Mesopotamian urban life.

leaders.name: William F. Albright
leaders.line: Johns Hopkins professor and the leading figure of 20th-century biblical archaeology.

leaders.name: Nelson Glueck
leaders.line: Rabbi and archaeologist whose surveys of Transjordan and the Negev mapped ancient settlements and trade routes.

leaders.name: Roland de Vaux
leaders.line: Directed excavations at Qumran and developed an influential, still debated interpretation of the settlement and Dead Sea Scrolls.

leaders.name: Olga Tufnell
leaders.line: Worked on the Lachish excavations and brought their Iron and Bronze Age finds into the final excavation reports.

leaders.name: Nahman Avigad
leaders.line: Excavated Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter and studied ancient Hebrew inscriptions, seals, and the material culture of the city.

leaders.name: Kathleen Kenyon
leaders.line: British archaeologist who excavated Jericho and Jerusalem and refined how digs are recorded layer by layer.

leaders.name: Benjamin Mazar
leaders.line: Combined historical geography with excavation at Tell Qasile, Beth Shearim, and the area south and west of Jerusalem's Temple Mount.

leaders.name: Kurt Bittel
leaders.line: Directed excavations at the Hittite capital Hattusha, documenting its architecture and material culture within the wider ancient Near East.

leaders.name: G. Ernest Wright
leaders.line: Archaeologist and biblical scholar who directed excavations at Shechem and wrote widely on archaeology and Israelite history.

leaders.name: Avraham Biran
leaders.line: Directed the long-running Tel Dan excavations, including the discovery of the inscription mentioning the House of David.

leaders.name: James B. Pritchard
leaders.line: Excavated Gibeon, Tell es-Sa'idiyeh, and Sarepta and edited ancient Near Eastern texts used to study the Bible's historical setting.

leaders.name: Yigael Yadin
leaders.line: Israeli archaeologist who excavated Hazor and Masada and published several of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

leaders.name: Trude Dothan
leaders.line: Specialist in Philistine material culture who excavated Deir el-Balah and co-directed the Tel Miqne-Ekron project.

leaders.name: William G. Dever
leaders.line: Excavator of Gezer and interpreter of ancient Israel whose work examines settlement, daily life, religion, and the relationship between archaeology and biblical texts.

leaders.name: Ehud Netzer
leaders.line: Archaeologist and architect who excavated Herodian palaces at Jericho, Masada, and Herodium and studied their construction and development.

leaders.name: David Ussishkin
leaders.line: Directed renewed excavations at Lachish and investigated its destruction levels, siege works, and relationship to Assyrian records.

leaders.name: Amnon Ben-Tor
leaders.line: Led the renewed Hazor excavations and edited reports on its Canaanite and Israelite remains, as well as a broad survey of Israel's archaeology.

leaders.name: Seymour Gitin
leaders.line: Co-directed the Tel Miqne-Ekron excavations and published research on Philistine industry, the Ekron inscription, and ceramic chronology.

leaders.name: Yigal Shiloh
leaders.line: Directed the City of David excavations and studied Israelite masonry, architecture, and the development of ancient Jerusalem.

leaders.name: Amihai Mazar
leaders.line: Archaeologist of ancient Israel whose excavations and synthesis examine settlement, chronology, and material culture.

leaders.name: Carol L. Meyers
leaders.line: Archaeologist of ancient Israel whose research combines household remains, social history, and biblical texts to study everyday life and women's activities.

leaders.name: Lawrence E. Stager
leaders.line: Directed the Leon Levy Expedition to Ashkelon, documenting the city's long history through excavation reports.

leaders.name: Ronny Reich
leaders.line: Excavated ancient Jerusalem with Eli Shukron and studied its water systems, the City of David, and Jewish ritual baths.

leaders.name: Israel Finkelstein
leaders.line: Archaeologist of the Levant whose surveys and contested chronological proposals have reshaped debate about ancient Israel.

leaders.name: William Lane Craig
leaders.line: Christian philosopher, theologian and debater whose apologetics writings examine the existence of God, the resurrection of Jesus, and faith and reason.
aliases: William Lane Craig & Shabir Ally · hosted by Reasonable Faith

leaders.name: Thomas E. Levy
leaders.line: Field archaeologist whose projects in Israel and Jordan combine excavation, radiocarbon dating, and metallurgy to study ancient societies and Edomite copper production.

leaders.name: Jodi Magness
leaders.line: Archaeologist of the Second Temple and early Roman periods whose work examines Qumran and the wider Holy Land.

leaders.name: Eilat Mazar
leaders.line: Directed excavations at the Ophel and City of David, publishing architectural remains, pottery, and seal impressions; some proposed building identifications remain debated.

leaders.name: Yosef Garfinkel
leaders.line: Excavator of Khirbet Qeiyafa and Lachish whose reports and interpretations contribute to debate about the emergence of the kingdom of Judah.

leaders.name: Aren M. Maeir
leaders.line: Directs the Tell es-Safi/Gath project, investigating Philistine culture, urban life, trade, and scientific methods of dating excavated contexts.

leaders.name: Eric H. Cline
leaders.line: Excavator at Megiddo and Tel Kabri whose books examine Bronze Age societies, archaeological methods, and the history of biblical archaeology.
